title: Classic Concurrency Problems
subtitle: FooBar, ZeroEvenOdd, FizzBuzz, H2O, philosophers, and six thread-safe designs

steps.say: Welcome to the L-L-D Workshop, episode fourteen: Classic Concurrency Problems. Last episode gave you the toolbox: locks, semaphores, condition variables, barriers and atomics. Today we use that toolbox on the exact problems interviewers ask.

By the end you'll be able to solve the five classic LeetCode concurrency puzzles, and design six thread-safe components in a machine-coding round: a cache with expiry, a concurrent hash map, a blocking queue, a Bloom filter, a parallel merge sort and a rate limiter.
Keep the chapter thirteen PDF open beside the video; it has the full Java code and real output.

scenes.title: A five-step checklist for any concurrency problem

steps.say: Here's a checklist for every problem today, applied right away to our first puzzle.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 Concurrency Problems · Reusable mental checklist

scenes.title: The concurrency checklist
bullets: 1. What is the shared state?
2. What ordering or invariant must hold?
3. Who waits, for what, and who signals?
4. Pick the primitive that fits
5. Check liveness: does everyone progress and exit?

steps.say: Step one, find the shared state. In FooBar, it's simply whose turn it is.
Step two, name the invariant, a rule that's always true. For FooBar: foo and bar strictly alternate.
Step three, who waits and who signals. The bar thread waits until foo has printed; foo signals it. Then the roles flip.
Step four, pick the primitive. Turn-taking, semaphores. Waiting for a condition, a condition variable. Groups, a barrier. Mutual exclusion, a lock. One variable, an atomic.
Step five, check liveness: can anyone wait forever, and does every thread exit? Most bugs hide here.

scenes.title: Print FooBar Alternately

steps.say: Problem one, LeetCode eleven fifteen. One object, two threads. Thread A calls foo and prints foo, n times. Thread B calls bar and prints bar, n times. The output must be foobar, foobar, foobar, whichever thread the scheduler starts first.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.1 Print FooBar Alternately

scenes.title: Approach: two semaphores as a baton
bullets: fooTurn starts with 1 permit, barTurn with 0
foo: acquire fooTurn, print, release barTurn
bar: acquire barTurn, print, release fooTurn
Alternative: one monitor plus a boolean turn flag

steps.say: Think of a relay baton. A semaphore counts permits: acquire takes one or waits, release gives one back. fooTurn starts with one permit, so foo may go first. barTurn starts with zero, so bar must wait.
The foo thread acquires its own semaphore, prints foo, then releases the other one, handing the baton to bar.
Bar is the mirror image: acquire barTurn, print bar, release fooTurn. The baton goes back.
You can also do it with one monitor: a boolean called fooTurn, a while loop that waits until it's your turn, then flip the flag and notify all.

scenes.title: The baton passing between threads
scenes.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as "foo thread"
    participant S as "semaphores"
    participant B as "bar thread"
    B->>S: barTurn.acquire waits
    A->>S: fooTurn.acquire ok
    A->>A: print foo
    A->>S: barTurn.release
    S-->>B: wakes
    B->>B: print bar
    B->>S: fooTurn.release
scenes.caption: One permit total, always held by exactly one side

steps.say: Here's the important case: the bar thread starts first, on purpose. It calls acquire on barTurn, which has zero permits, so it simply blocks. Foo acquires, prints, releases barTurn. Bar wakes, prints, releases fooTurn. Order is forced no matter who starts.

scenes.title: Example: n equals 2, bar thread starts first

steps.say: Let's trace n equals two. At the start, fooTurn has one permit and barTurn has zero. Add them: one.
Bar starts first and blocks, because barTurn is zero.
Foo acquires its permit, so both are zero for a moment, and prints foo.
Foo releases barTurn. Total permits: one again.
Bar wakes, prints bar, releases fooTurn. We have foobar.
Round two repeats exactly. The total is always one, so at most one thread prints at a time, and they strictly alternate.

scenes.title: Why it's correct, and the pitfalls

left.heading: Correct because
bullets: Permits across both semaphores always total 1
Release happens-before the acquire it enables
Each loop runs n times; every acquire is matched

right.heading: Pitfalls
bullets: One shared semaphore: a thread re-takes its own permit
if instead of while in the monitor version
Busy-waiting on a volatile flag burns a core

steps.say: The invariant: total permits are always exactly one.
Visibility is free. In the Java memory model, a release happens-before the acquire it enables, so bar sees everything foo wrote.
Termination: both loops run exactly n times, and every acquire has a matching release, so both threads exit.
Pitfall one: using a single semaphore for both. A thread can release and then immediately grab its own permit back, and print foo twice.
Pitfall two: an if instead of a while in the monitor version, which breaks on spurious wake-ups.
Pitfall three: spinning on a volatile flag burns a whole C-P-U core. Real-world cousins: ping-pong protocols and double-buffering.

scenes.title: In the interview: FooBar
scenes.caption: Follow-up: three threads A, B, C? A ring of three semaphores

steps.say: Say this: two semaphores as a baton; foo's starts at one, bar's at zero; each thread acquires its own, prints, and releases the other's; total permits are always one, so they alternate. If they ask for three threads printing A, B, C, use three semaphores in a ring, A at one, B and C at zero, each releasing the next.

scenes.title: Print Zero Even Odd

steps.say: Problem two, LeetCode eleven sixteen. Three threads share one object. One may only print zero, one only even numbers, one only odd numbers. Together they must print zero one, zero two, zero three, up to n. For n equals five that's zero one zero two zero three zero four zero five.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.2 Print Zero Even Odd

scenes.title: Approach: zero is the dispatcher
bullets: Semaphores: zeroTurn 1, oddTurn 0, evenTurn 0
zero: acquire zeroTurn, print 0, release odd or even
odd and even: acquire own, print number, release zeroTurn
Loop counts: zero n, odd ceil(n/2), even floor(n/2)

steps.say: Three semaphores. Zero starts with the only permit.
The zero thread is a dispatcher, a coordinator that decides who goes next. For position i, it prints zero, then releases oddTurn if i is odd, or evenTurn if i is even.
That thread prints its number and hands control straight back through zeroTurn.
The loop counts must match the permits each thread receives. Zero loops n times. Odd loops over one, three, five. Even over two, four, six.

scenes.title: Example: n equals 4, step by step

steps.say: Let's walk n equals four. i is one: zero prints zero, one is odd, so it releases oddTurn. Odd prints one and releases zeroTurn.
i is two: zero prints zero, releases evenTurn, even prints two.
i is three: odd again, prints three.

i is four: even prints four. Output: zero one zero two zero three zero four. So how many times did odd acquire? Twice, for one and three. Even also twice. And for n equals one, even's loop runs zero times and exits cleanly.

left.heading: Correct because
bullets: Exactly one semaphore holds a permit at any moment
Zero's index i decides the parity of the next number
Loop counts equal permits received: nobody hangs

right.heading: Pitfalls
bullets: Workers computing 'next number' from an unsynced counter
Loop bounds that don't match permits: program hangs

steps.say: One permit circulates among three semaphores, so exactly one thread prints at a time.
The dispatcher's index picks the right worker.
Every thread gets exactly as many permits as loop iterations, so everyone exits.
Pitfall: letting odd and even compute the next number from a shared counter without synchronization.

Pitfall: off-by-one loop bounds. If even loops one time too many, it waits forever and the program hangs. Real systems use this dispatcher-worker shape, like an interpreter routing instructions. In the interview: zero dispatches, one permit circulates.

scenes.title: Fizz Buzz Multithreaded

steps.say: Problem three, LeetCode eleven ninety-five. Four threads together print one to n. Multiples of fifteen print fizzbuzz. Multiples of three only print fizz. Multiples of five only print buzz. Everything else prints the number. Each kind belongs to a different thread.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.3 Fizz Buzz Multithreaded

scenes.title: Approach: shared counter plus per-thread predicate
bullets: One counter 'current', guarded by the object's monitor
Wait while current is not mine and not past n
If current is past n: notifyAll and exit
Else print, increment, notifyAll
One helper runWhile(predicate, action) for all four

steps.say: This is the condition-variable pattern. A predicate is a yes-or-no test. There's one shared counter called current, and every read and write happens inside synchronized on the object.
Step one: each thread waits in a while loop while current is not its number and still not past n.
Step two: if current has passed n, notify all and exit, so the others wake up and exit too.
Step three: otherwise print, increment current, and notify all, because the next number might belong to anyone.
All four threads share one helper that takes a predicate and an action. That's DRY, don't repeat yourself.
Take n equals fifteen. At thirteen, only the number thread's predicate is true, so it prints and notifies all. The other three wake, check, and go back to waiting.
Same for fourteen.
At fifteen, only fizzbuzz matches. Notice fizz's predicate is divisible by three and not by five, so it does not claim fifteen.
Current becomes sixteen, past n. The last notify all wakes everyone, each sees current past n, and all four exit. The predicates partition the numbers: each number satisfies exactly one.

scenes.title: Why notifyAll here, and not notify?
bullets: A. notify is slower
B. notify might wake the wrong thread, and the right one never wakes
C. notify doesn't release the lock

steps.say: Pause and think. Four threads wait on one monitor for four different conditions. Which answer is right?

scenes.title: Answer: B. Plus the other pitfalls

left.heading: Correct because
bullets: Predicates partition 1..n: one thread per number
current only touched inside synchronized
notifyAll guarantees the right thread wakes

right.heading: Pitfalls
bullets: notify(): lost wake-ups, random hangs
No 'past n' exit check: threads wait forever
Overlapping predicates: two threads fight over 15

steps.say: Answer B. With notify, Java might wake the fizz thread when the number belongs to buzz. Fizz checks, goes back to sleep, and buzz is never woken. The program hangs.
And because current is only touched inside the lock, there are no races and visibility is guaranteed.
Notify all wakes every waiter, so the right one always gets a chance.
Pitfalls: notify instead of notify all.
Forgetting the past-n exit check, so threads sleep forever after the last number.

Or overlapping predicates. Real-world cousin: pipeline stages, each waiting until a job reaches its stage. A semaphore version avoids the thundering herd, where many threads wake but only one can proceed, at the cost of more code.

scenes.title: Building H2O

steps.say: Problem four, LeetCode eleven seventeen. Hydrogen and oxygen threads arrive in any order. They must leave in groups of three, each forming one water molecule: exactly two H and one O. All three atoms of one molecule must leave before any atom of the next.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.4 Building H2O

scenes.title: Approach: slots decide who, a barrier decides when
bullets: hSlots = Semaphore(2): at most 2 H per molecule
oSlots = Semaphore(1): at most 1 O per molecule
CyclicBarrier(3): the three atoms wait for each other
Return your slot only AFTER you've been released

steps.say: Two kinds of tool. First, slots. The hydrogen semaphore has two permits, so at most two hydrogens are inside the current molecule.
The oxygen semaphore has one permit.
Second, a cyclic barrier of three. A barrier holds threads until all three parties arrive, then lets them all go. Cyclic means it resets itself for the next round.
The crucial detail: a thread gives its slot back only after it has printed and left. That way the next molecule can't form until this one is finished.

scenes.title: H2O flow
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    H["H thread"] --> HS["hSlots acquire, max 2"]
    O["O thread"] --> OS["oSlots acquire, max 1"]
    HS --> BAR["CyclicBarrier 3 await"]
    OS --> BAR
    BAR --> REL["release and print"]
    REL --> BACK["give slot back"]
scenes.caption: Slots cap the group; the barrier releases it together

steps.say: Follow the arrows. An H thread grabs one of two H slots, an O thread grabs the single O slot. All of them meet at the barrier. When the third arrives, all three print, and only then return their slots.

scenes.title: Example: arrivals O, H, O, H, H

head: Arrival
What happens
rows: takes the only O slot, waits at barrier (1 of 3)
takes H slot 1, waits at barrier (2 of 3)
no O slot free, blocks on oSlots
takes H slot 2, barrier trips: H1 H2 O1 print
O2 gets the O slot; H3 joins the next molecule

steps.say: Imagine arrivals O, H, O, H, H. The first oxygen takes the only O slot and waits at the barrier, one of three.
The first hydrogen takes an H slot. Two of three.
The second oxygen can't get in. No O slot is free, so it blocks on the semaphore and never reaches the barrier.
The second hydrogen arrives, three of three, the barrier trips, and H, H, O print together.
Only after printing do they return slots. Now the waiting oxygen and the third hydrogen start molecule two.

left.heading: Correct because
bullets: Slots let at most 2 H and 1 O reach the barrier
Barrier needs 3, so each trip is exactly H, H, O
Slots freed after printing: no mixing

right.heading: Pitfalls
bullets: Release slot before printing: molecules interleave
Semaphores without barrier: atoms don't leave together
Counts not exactly 2 to 1: last threads wait forever

steps.say: The semaphores cap who can reach the barrier.
The barrier needs three, so every trip is exactly two H and one O.
And because slots return only after printing, the next group can't print until the previous one is done.
Pitfall: freeing the slot before printing. A new hydrogen could print before the old oxygen.
Pitfall: semaphores alone, with no barrier. Nothing forces the three to leave together.

And if the thread counts aren't exactly two to one, the leftovers wait forever. Real-world, this is batching: matchmaking two players plus a server slot, or assembling an order from parts. In the interview: slots decide who joins, the barrier decides when they leave.

scenes.title: Dining Philosophers

steps.say: Problem five, the most famous one, LeetCode twelve twenty-six. Five philosophers sit at a round table with one fork between each pair, five forks total. To eat, you need both adjacent forks.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.5 Dining Philosophers

steps.say: Philosopher p uses fork p on the left and fork p plus one on the right, wrapping around, so philosopher four uses forks four and zero.

Now imagine everyone picks up their left fork at the same instant. Each holds one fork and waits forever for the next. That's deadlock. All four Coffman conditions hold: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break any one and deadlock is impossible.

scenes.title: Three ways to break the deadlock
bullets: 1. Resource ordering: always take the lower-numbered fork
2. Waiter: a semaphore lets only n minus 1 try at once
3. tryLock both forks, back off randomly on failure

steps.say: Fix one, resource ordering. Number the forks zero to four and always pick up the lower number first. Philosophers zero to three behave normally. But philosopher four, between forks four and zero, picks up fork zero first. That one person breaking the pattern makes a cycle impossible.

Fix two, a waiter. A semaphore with four seats lets at most four of the five try at once. Four people, five forks: by the pigeonhole principle, at least one gets both forks, eats and frees them. Make the semaphore fair, first come first served, so nobody starves waiting for a seat.

Fix three, try-lock. Try both forks; if you can't get the second, put the first down, wait a random short time, and retry. That breaks hold-and-wait instead. Without the random back-off you risk livelock: everyone politely retrying in lockstep forever.

scenes.title: Example: everyone grabs at once, with ordering

steps.say: Let's replay the disaster with ordering on. Philosopher zero wants fork zero first.
Philosopher one takes fork one and waits for two.
Philosopher two takes two and waits for three.
Philosopher three takes fork three, and fork four is free, because philosopher four never picks four first. So philosopher three eats, then frees forks three and four, and the chain unblocks.

Philosopher four competes with zero for fork zero. One of them waits; nobody holds a higher fork while waiting for a lower one, so no cycle. In the demo, all five philosophers eat ten thousand meals each under both fixes, with no hangs.

scenes.title: Where you'll meet this, and what to say

left.heading: Real world
bullets: Bank transfer: lock two accounts by id order
Moving stock between two inventories
Databases: detect deadlock, abort one transaction

right.heading: In the interview
bullets: Naive left-then-right: circular wait, deadlock
Ordering or n minus 1 waiter breaks circular wait
Fair semaphore or fair locks stop starvation

steps.say: Any code needing two locks at once is dining philosophers. A bank transfer locks two accounts: lower id first.
Moving stock between two inventories too.
Databases instead detect the deadlock and abort one transaction.
In the interview: naive left-then-right is circular wait.
Break it with a global fork order, or a waiter allowing n minus one diners.
Fairness prevents starvation. And with five forks, at most two can eat at once.

scenes.title: Which Coffman condition does tryLock with back-off break?
bullets: A. Mutual exclusion
B. Hold-and-wait
C. Circular wait

steps.say: Pause and think. Ordering and the waiter both break circular wait. What does try-lock break?

scenes.title: Thread-safe cache with TTL

steps.say: The answer was B, hold-and-wait: if you can't get the second fork, you put the first one down, so you never hold while waiting. Now we switch from puzzles to machine coding: design a thread-safe X.

Problem six: an in-memory cache, a fast store of copies, used by many threads, where every entry expires after a time-to-live, or T-T-L. Requirements: get returns nothing for expired entries; getOrLoad loads on a miss without a stampede; expired entries eventually leave memory; and it's testable without sleeping.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.6 Thread-safe cache with TTL

scenes.title: Approach: five design decisions
bullets: Immutable Entry(value, expiresAt) in a ConcurrentHashMap
Lazy expiry: get checks, then remove(key, entry)
Active expiry: a daemon sweeper every few milliseconds
No stampede: getOrLoad uses map.compute
Injected Ticker clock, so tests use a fake clock

steps.say: One: store immutable entries, a value plus an expiry time, in a concurrent hash map. A reader sees the old entry or the new one, never a half-written one.

Two: lazy expiry. On get, check the expiry. If expired, remove it with the conditional remove, key and entry, which deletes only if the map still holds that exact entry. If another thread just put a fresh value, it survives.
Three: active expiry. A daemon thread, one that doesn't keep the program alive, sweeps expired entries on a timer, so keys nobody reads again don't leak memory.

Four: no cache stampede. A stampede is many threads all loading the same missing key at once. compute runs atomically per key, so concurrent misses wait and the loader runs once. This is called single-flight.
Five: time comes from an injected Ticker interface, so tests use a fake clock you can advance. That's dependency inversion.

scenes.title: Example: login sessions and one-time passwords

head: Time
Action
Result
rows: getOrLoad user 7 at the same instant

steps.say: Imagine a login service. At time zero we store alice's session with a one hundred millisecond T-T-L, and a one-time password, an O-T-P, with thirty.
Advance the fake clock to fifty milliseconds. The session is still there; the O-T-P has expired.
At one hundred ten milliseconds the session is gone too.
Now sixteen threads, released together by a latch, all call getOrLoad for user seven. The loader runs exactly once and all sixteen get the same value. No stampede.
With a real clock, a thousand short-lived puts are all gone after two hundred milliseconds, thanks to the sweeper.

left.heading: Pitfalls
bullets: currentTimeMillis can jump; use monotonic nanoTime
Slow loader inside compute blocks a whole bin
Lazy only leaks; active only serves stale data
No max size: needs an LRU or LFU eviction policy

right.heading: Real world
bullets: Caffeine: the production Java version
Redis EXPIRE: lazy plus periodic sampling
Sessions, OTPs, DNS caches, seat holds

steps.say: Pitfall one: wall-clock time can jump when the network time protocol corrects it. nanoTime only moves forward.
Pitfall two: a slow loader inside compute blocks other keys in that bin. Store a CompletableFuture, a placeholder filled later, instead.
Pitfall three: lazy alone leaks; active alone serves stale values between sweeps. Use both.
Pitfall four: no size limit. A real cache evicts by L-R-U, least recently used, or L-F-U, least frequently used.
The real-world version is Caffeine, the standard Java caching library.
Redis does the same mix: lazy expiry on access plus periodic sampling.
Plus sessions, D-N-S caches and seat holds. In the interview: concurrent map of immutable entries, lazy plus scheduled expiry, compute for single-flight, injected clock.

scenes.title: A simplified ConcurrentHashMap

steps.say: Problem seven: build a hash map many threads can use at once, with get, put, remove, compute and automatic resizing, faster than one global lock around a HashMap. The technique is lock striping: N locks, each guarding its own slice of the data.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.7 Simplified Concurrent HashMap, lock striping

scenes.title: Approach: lock striping step by step
bullets: Buckets: array of linked lists (separate chaining)
Stripes: S locks, S a power of two
stripe = h AND (S - 1); bucket = h AND (length - 1)
Each operation locks only its own stripe
Resize: take ALL stripe locks in order, rehash, publish
Size kept in an AtomicInteger

steps.say: Buckets are an array of linked lists. Separate chaining means each bucket lists all entries whose hash lands there.
Next to that, a small fixed array of S locks, where S is a power of two, say sixteen.

For hash h, the stripe is h AND S minus one, the low bits. The bucket is h AND table length minus one. The key point: the stripe depends only on the hash, not on the table length, so a key's lock never changes when the table grows.
Every operation locks just its stripe, so threads on different stripes run in parallel.

Resize happens when size passes zero point seven five times the bucket count. Take every stripe lock in index order, which avoids deadlock, re-check, rehash into a table twice as big, publish it through a volatile field, and unlock in reverse.
Size is an atomic integer.

scenes.title: From key to lock to bucket
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart TB
    K["key"] --> H["spread hashCode"]
    H --> S["stripe = h AND S-1"]
    H --> B["bucket = h AND len-1"]
    S --> L["lock stripe"]
    L --> B
    B --> C["walk chain, update, unlock"]
scenes.caption: Every bucket belongs to exactly one stripe

steps.say: Here's the path. Spread the hash code by mixing in its high bits. Use the low bits to pick a stripe and lock it. Then use the low bits again to pick a bucket, walk the chain, update, unlock.

Let's do numbers. Four stripes, sixteen buckets, a key with hash forty-five. Bucket: forty-five AND fifteen is thirteen. Stripe: forty-five AND three is one. And notice thirteen AND three is also one: the stripe is just the low bits of the bucket index, so every key in bucket thirteen shares stripe one.
Grow to thirty-two buckets: still bucket thirteen, still stripe one.

Grow to sixty-four: now bucket forty-five, but still stripe one. The key's lock never moved. In the demo, eight threads doing twenty thousand puts each end with exactly one hundred sixty thousand entries.

left.heading: Correct because
bullets: S divides length: one bucket, one stripe
Resize holds every lock, re-checks, volatile publish
Normal ops hold 1 lock; resize takes all in order

right.heading: Pitfalls
bullets: Stripe from current bucket index: lock moves on resize
Resizing while holding a stripe: deadlock
Reading table without lock or volatile: stale table
Allowing null keys or values: get is ambiguous

steps.say: Because both sizes are powers of two and S is at most the table length, every bucket maps to exactly one stripe. Two threads never edit the same chain.
Resize holds every lock, so nothing else runs. It re-checks the load because another thread may already have resized, and the volatile write publishes the new table.
No deadlock: normal operations hold one lock. Resize takes all of them in order, and only after the caller has released its own stripe.
Pitfall: deriving the stripe from the current bucket index. After a resize a key can move to a different lock while some thread holds the old one.
Pitfall: calling resize while still holding your stripe. Two resizers would deadlock.
Pitfall: reading the table field without a lock or volatile, so you see a stale table.
And allowing nulls. If get returns null, does that mean absent or a null value? The real ConcurrentHashMap forbids nulls for exactly this reason.

scenes.title: How the real ConcurrentHashMap goes further

head: Aspect
Our striped map
JDK 8+ ConcurrentHashMap
rows: CAS into empty bin, else lock bin head

steps.say: Java seven's ConcurrentHashMap used our idea, with sixteen segments. Java eight goes further: reads take no lock at all.
Writes into an empty bin use compare-and-swap, C-A-S; otherwise they lock just that bin's first node, a lock per bucket.
A chain longer than eight nodes becomes a red-black tree, so lookups stay fast even with bad hashes.
Resize is incremental: threads touching the map help move bins, instead of everyone pausing.
And size uses spread-out counter cells. In the interview: N locks for M buckets, stripe by hash bits, resize under all locks in order, publish through volatile.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.7 How the real ConcurrentHashMap goes further

scenes.title: Bounded blocking queue, two ways

steps.say: Problem eight: a fixed-capacity, first-in-first-out queue for producers and consumers. put blocks while it's full, take blocks while it's empty, and timed versions, offer and poll, give up after a timeout.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.8 Thread-safe bounded Blocking Queue

scenes.title: Storage: a circular array
bullets: items array, plus head, tail and count
enqueue: write at tail, tail = (tail + 1) mod capacity
dequeue: read at head, null the slot, advance head
Wait while full or empty, always in a while loop

steps.say: The storage is a circular array, also called a ring buffer: when you reach the end you wrap to the start. Three fields: head, tail and count.
Enqueue writes at tail, then moves tail forward, wrapping with modulo capacity, and increments count.
Dequeue reads at head, sets that slot to null so the garbage collector can reclaim the object, moves head forward and decrements count.
Producers wait while count equals capacity; consumers wait while count is zero. Always in a while loop, for spurious wake-ups and for when another thread got there first.

scenes.title: Queue states
scenes.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Empty
    Empty --> Partial : put
    Partial --> Partial : put or take
    Partial --> Full : put reaches capacity
    Full --> Partial : take
    Partial --> Empty : take last item
scenes.caption: take waits in Empty; put waits in Full

steps.say: Three states: empty, partial and full. In empty, take waits. In full, put waits. Every other move is immediate.

scenes.title: Way 1 monitor versus Way 2 Lock plus Conditions

left.heading: Way 1: synchronized
bullets: while (full) wait()
notifyAll: producers and consumers share one wait set
Wakes everyone: thundering herd

right.heading: Way 2: ReentrantLock
bullets: Two Conditions: notFull and notEmpty
while (full) notFull.await()
signal() wakes exactly one of the right kind

steps.say: Way one: synchronized methods. Wait while full or empty.
But producers and consumers sleep in the same wait set, so you must notify all. A plain notify might wake another producer when a consumer was needed, and the right thread never wakes.
The cost: everyone wakes on every change, a thundering herd.
Way two, how Java's ArrayBlockingQueue is built: one reentrant lock with two condition queues, notFull and notEmpty.
Producers wait only on notFull, consumers only on notEmpty.
So after an enqueue you signal notEmpty, waking exactly one consumer, and after a dequeue you signal notFull. Targeted signal is safe because each queue holds only one kind of waiter.
Imagine a logging pipeline, capacity two, three producer threads, one consumer. Producer one puts log A. Count one.
Producer two puts B. Count two, full.
Producer three tries to put C and waits on notFull.
The consumer takes A. Dequeue signals notFull, waking only producer three.
Producer three re-checks the while condition, finds room, puts C, and signals notEmpty.
And for timeouts: poll for thirty milliseconds on an empty queue returns null. awaitNanos returns the time left, so spurious wake-ups can't stretch the total wait.

left.heading: Pitfalls
bullets: if instead of while; notify with one shared monitor
Forgetting items[head] = null: memory leak
Accepting null when null means 'timed out'
lock() instead of lockInterruptibly()

right.heading: Real world
bullets: ArrayBlockingQueue: exactly Way 2
LinkedBlockingQueue: separate put and take locks
Thread pools, loggers, Kafka producer internals

steps.say: Pitfalls: if instead of while, and notify with one shared monitor.
Forgetting to null out the dequeued slot, so the array keeps big objects alive.
Accepting null items when your poll uses null to mean timed out.
And plain lock instead of lockInterruptibly, which makes cancelling a blocked thread harder.
ArrayBlockingQueue is exactly way two.
LinkedBlockingQueue uses two locks, one for put and one for take, so a producer and consumer can work at the same moment. That's your answer if they ask for higher throughput.
Thread pools, loggers and Kafka's producer rely on it. In the interview: circular buffer, one lock, wait in loops; monitor means notify all, Lock means two conditions.

scenes.title: Concurrent Bloom filter

steps.say: Problem nine: a Bloom filter that many threads add to and query at once. A Bloom filter is a tiny probabilistic set. It answers either definitely not present, or probably present.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.9 Concurrent Bloom Filter

scenes.title: How a Bloom filter works
bullets: 1. An array of m bits, all 0
2. Add: compute k hash positions, set those bits to 1
3. Query: any of the k bits is 0 = definitely absent
4. All k bits are 1 = probably present
No false negatives, no deletion

steps.say: Step one: start with m bits, all zero.
Step two, add: hash the item to k positions and set those bits. Double hashing makes this cheap: compute two hashes once, then use h one plus i times h two for i from zero to k minus one.
Step three, query: check the same k positions. If any bit is zero, this item was definitely never added.
Step four: if all are one, it was probably added, because other items might have set those bits. That's a false positive.
There are never false negatives. And you can't delete, because clearing a bit might erase other items. A counting Bloom filter, with small counters instead of bits, does support deletes.

scenes.title: Example: sizing for 80,000 usernames
scenes.caption: About 9.6 bits per item, about 94 kibibytes total

steps.say: Imagine a sign-up page checking whether a username is taken, before hitting the database. We expect n equals eighty thousand names and want a false-positive rate p of one percent. The formula for bits is minus n times the natural log of p, divided by the natural log of two, squared. That gives seven hundred sixty-six thousand eight hundred five bits, about ninety-four kibibytes. Hashes k is m over n times the natural log of two, which rounds to seven. That's about nine point six bits per item, no matter how long the names are. In the demo, the measured false-positive rate is one point zero one percent, right on target.

left.heading: The trick
bullets: Bits in an AtomicLongArray, 64 per word
Set a bit with atomic OR: getAndAccumulate
Queries are plain volatile reads
Bits only go 0 to 1: monotonic

right.heading: Why plain OR fails
bullets: words[i] |= mask is read, modify, write
Two threads, same word: one bit is lost
Lost bit means a false negative

steps.say: Store the bits in an atomic long array, sixty-four bits per word.
Set a bit with an atomic OR, getAndAccumulate, which is a compare-and-swap loop inside. Two threads setting different bits in the same word both succeed.
Queries need no lock. They're just volatile reads.

Because bits only ever go from zero to one, the state is monotonic. A query racing with an unfinished add can at worst miss it, which is fine, since that add hadn't happened yet. And OR is commutative, so the final bits are identical whatever the interleaving.
Now why does the plain version break? words at i, OR-equals mask, is three steps: read, modify, write.
Thread one reads the word, thread two reads the same word, both write back. One thread's bit is overwritten.
And a lost bit means a false negative, the one thing a Bloom filter must never produce.

scenes.title: Pitfalls, real world, interview line
bullets: Weak hashes cluster bits: mix with FNV-1a plus Murmur finalizer
Adding far more than n: false positives climb fast
Cassandra, HBase, RocksDB: skip disk reads per SSTable
Guava BloomFilter, RedisBloom BF.ADD and BF.EXISTS

steps.say: Pitfalls: weak hashes, like String hashCode with small offsets, cluster the bits and push false positives way up. Mix the bits with strong, fast hashes like F-N-V one-A and the MurmurHash finalizer.
And overfilling: past n items the false-positive rate climbs fast. Build a bigger filter, or chain filters.
Real world: Cassandra, HBase, RocksDB and LevelDB keep a Bloom filter per S-S-Table, a sorted file on disk, to skip disk reads for keys that aren't there.
Guava's BloomFilter uses atomic long arrays like this, and Redis has BF dot ADD. In the interview: no is certain, yes is probable, atomic OR is lock-free and correct.

scenes.title: Multi-threaded merge sort with Fork/Join

steps.say: Problem ten: sort a big integer array using all your C-P-U cores. Merge sort is divide and conquer: sort both halves independently, then merge. Independent halves means they can run in parallel. Java's Fork Join framework is built exactly for this.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.10 Multi-threaded Merge Sort (Fork/Join)

scenes.title: Approach: four steps
bullets: 1. Range of 8,192 or less: Arrays.sort it sequentially
2. Else split at mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1, invokeAll both
3. Merge with ONE shared scratch buffer, own range only
4. Work stealing keeps every core busy

steps.say: Step one, the threshold. If the range has eight thousand one hundred ninety-two elements or fewer, just sort it sequentially. Below that, splitting costs more than it saves.
Step two: split at the midpoint. Use an unsigned shift right by one instead of dividing by two, so huge indexes can't overflow. invokeAll forks both halves and waits for both.
Step three: merge using one scratch buffer allocated once. Each task touches only its own slice, so concurrent tasks share nothing.
Step four: work stealing. Every pool thread has its own deque of tasks. An idle thread steals from the far end of a busy thread's deque, so all cores stay busy.

scenes.title: Split, sort small pieces, merge back up
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart TB
    A["sort 0..N"] --> B["sort 0..N/2"]
    A --> C["sort N/2..N"]
    B --> D["small: Arrays.sort"]
    B --> E["small: Arrays.sort"]
    C --> F["small: Arrays.sort"]
    C --> G["small: Arrays.sort"]
    D --> M1["merge"]
    E --> M1
    F --> M2["merge"]
    G --> M2
scenes.caption: Children finish before the parent merges

steps.say: Read it top down for splitting and bottom up for merging. Four leaves sort in parallel, two merges run in parallel, then one final merge.
Imagine sorting four million random integers on an eight-core laptop. One task covers everything.
Level one: two tasks of two million.
Level five: thirty-two tasks, more than cores, and work stealing balances them.

Level nine: five hundred twelve leaves of about seven thousand eight hundred each, under the threshold, so each just calls Arrays dot sort. Then merges climb back up, and the result matches Arrays dot sort.

left.heading: Correct because
bullets: Subtasks touch disjoint ranges: no data race
invokeAll and join give happens-before
Ties take from the left run: a stable sort

right.heading: Pitfalls
bullets: No threshold: millions of tiny tasks
New buffer per merge: heavy garbage collection
Blocking I/O inside Fork/Join tasks
Amdahl: the final merge is sequential

steps.say: Disjoint ranges of the array and the buffer mean no locks are needed.
invokeAll returns only when both children finish, and join gives happens-before, so the parent sees the children's writes.
On ties, take from the left. That keeps the sort stable, meaning equal elements keep their order, which matters for objects.
Pitfall: no threshold, so overhead swamps the work.
A new buffer per merge, and the garbage collector drowns.
Blocking I-O inside Fork Join tasks. The pool is for C-P-U work.

And Amdahl's law: the sequential part, here the final merge, caps your speed-up. Real world: Arrays dot parallelSort and parallel streams run on the same common pool, and Spark and MapReduce do divide-sort-merge across machines. In the interview: split until small, sort sequentially, merge, disjoint ranges, no locks.

scenes.title: Token-bucket rate limiter, thread-safe

steps.say: The last problem: a rate limiter for an A-P-I, an application programming interface. Allow short bursts up to B requests, and a sustained rate of R per second, per client, correctly under many concurrent requests.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.11 Rate limiter, token bucket

scenes.title: The token bucket, step by step
bullets: 1. Bucket holds up to capacity tokens, starts full
2. Tokens drip in at refillRate per second, capped
3. Each request takes one token; none means HTTP 429
4. Refill lazily: tokens += elapsed times rate

steps.say: Step one: a bucket holds up to capacity tokens. Capacity is your allowed burst. It starts full.
Step two: tokens drip in at the refill rate, never above capacity.
Step three: every request takes one token. No token? Reject with H-T-T-P four twenty-nine, too many requests.
Step four: refill lazily. Store just two numbers, tokens and lastRefill. On each request add elapsed time times rate. No background thread at all.
Imagine a weather A-P-I, capacity five, refill two per second. At time zero, seven requests: five pass, two rejected.
One second later, two new tokens have dripped in. Three requests: two pass, one rejected.
At one point two five seconds, only half a token has accumulated. Rejected.
At one point five seconds, a full token. Allowed.
Then the client goes idle for an hour, and a hundred requests arrive at the same instant. Only five pass, because tokens are capped at capacity. The burst never exceeds five.

left.heading: 1. synchronized
bullets: Refill, check and take inside one method
Simple and correct

right.heading: 2. Lock-free CAS
bullets: Immutable State(tokens, lastRefill)
Held in one AtomicReference
Compute next state, compareAndSet, retry
Clamp now so time never goes backwards

steps.say: Here's the race to avoid: if refill, check and take are separate steps, two threads both see one token and both take it. They must be one atomic step.
Version one: make tryAcquire synchronized. Simple and correct.
Version two, lock-free. Put tokens and lastRefill together in one immutable State record.
Keep it in an atomic reference. That's the trick: several fields, one immutable object, one C-A-S.
Read the current state, compute the next one, and compareAndSet. If another thread changed it first, the C-A-S fails and you recompute. Each token is granted at most once.
And clamp now to at least lastRefill, so a thread that read the clock slightly earlier can't move time backwards.

scenes.title: Per client, pitfalls, and many servers

left.heading: Per client
bullets: ConcurrentHashMap: client id to bucket
computeIfAbsent: exactly one bucket per client
alice spams YYYn, bob still gets YY

right.heading: Pitfalls
bullets: Separate refill() and take(): token spent twice
A timer thread per bucket: thousands of threads
Unbounded bucket map: evict idle ones with a TTL
In-memory is per server: use Redis plus Lua

steps.say: Per client, keep a concurrent hash map from client id, like a user id, A-P-I key or I-P address, to a bucket.
computeIfAbsent is atomic, so two simultaneous first requests can't create two buckets and double the limit.
With a burst of three, alice spams four requests and gets yes, yes, yes, no, and bob still gets his yes, yes. Alice's spam doesn't hurt bob.
Pitfalls: a separate refill and take means a token spent twice.
A background timer per bucket means thousands of threads; lazy refill needs none.
An unbounded map of buckets leaks memory; evict idle buckets, for example with our T-T-L cache from problem six.

And an in-memory limiter only limits per server. For a global limit across ten servers, keep the bucket in Redis and update it atomically with a Lua script, which Redis runs as one uninterruptible step.
Token bucket is the most common for A-P-Is. Stripe has described using token buckets backed by Redis, and Amazon A-P-I Gateway throttling is configured with exactly a rate and a burst.
Leaky bucket smooths traffic to a constant output rate. The engine-X web server's request limiter works this way.
Fixed window counter is simplest, but allows double the burst at window edges.
Sliding window log is exact but stores a timestamp per request.
Sliding window counter is a good compromise. In the interview: capacity for burst, rate for average, lazy refill, atomic refill-check-take, one bucket per client, Redis across servers.

scenes.title: Chapter summary and self-check

steps.say: That's all eleven. For each one, the single most valuable thing to say in an interview is its invariant. Here they are side by side.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 13 · 13.12 Chapter summary, 13.13 self-check, 13.14 TL;DR

head: Problem
Primitive
Invariant to state
rows: 2 H, 1 O; slot freed after release
load once; one stripe per bucket
count in range; bits 0 to 1; disjoint; atomic take

steps.say: FooBar and Zero Even Odd: exactly one permit circulates.
FizzBuzz: the predicates partition one to n.
H-two-O: at most two H and one O per round, and slots are freed only after release.
Philosophers: no circular wait.
T-T-L cache: never return expired data, and load once per key. Striped map: each bucket belongs to exactly one stripe.

Blocking queue: count stays between zero and capacity, and you wait in loops. Bloom filter: bits only go zero to one, so no false negatives. Merge sort: subtasks touch disjoint ranges. Rate limiter: refill plus take is one atomic step.

scenes.title: Why must a stripe depend only on the hash?
bullets: A. It's faster to compute
B. So a key's lock doesn't change when the table resizes
C. So the map can store nulls

steps.say: Quick self-check from the chapter. Pause and answer, then I'll go through more.

scenes.title: Self-check answers
bullets: Striped map: B, a key's lock must survive a resize
FooBar: start order doesn't matter, the other blocks
H2O: free the slot after printing, so molecules don't mix
TTL cache: remove(key, entry) keeps a fresh value
signal() is safe when one change enables exactly one waiter
Global token bucket on 10 servers: Redis plus Lua

steps.say: The answer is B. If the stripe came from the bucket index, a resize could move a key to a different lock while someone holds the old one.
In FooBar, why doesn't start order matter? The thread without a permit just blocks until the other releases.
In H-two-O, why free the slot after printing? So the next molecule can't form until this one has left.
Why does the T-T-L cache use remove with key and entry? So it never deletes a fresh value another thread just wrote.
When is a single signal safe? When each condition queue holds one kind of waiter, and each change enables exactly one of them.
And a token bucket across ten servers? Redis, updated atomically by a Lua script.

scenes.title: Chapter TL;DR
bullets: Ordering puzzles: semaphores as batons, barriers for groups
Predicate waiting: lock + while-wait + notifyAll or signal
Multi-lock: break circular wait by ordering or limiting
Data structures: immutable entries, CAS, striping, clocks
Parallel algorithms: Fork/Join, threshold, disjoint data

steps.say: Let's recap the whole episode in five lines. Ordering puzzles, FooBar, Zero Even Odd and H-two-O: semaphores as batons, barriers for groups, and exactly-one-permit invariants.
Predicate waiting, FizzBuzz and the blocking queue: a lock, a while loop around wait or await, and notify all or a targeted signal.
Multi-lock problems like the dining philosophers: break circular wait with ordering or by limiting who tries.

Thread-safe data structures, the cache, map, queue, Bloom filter and rate limiter: immutable entries, atomic compound operations, striping, C-A-S on immutable state, and injected clocks so time is testable.
Parallel algorithms like merge sort: Fork Join with a threshold and disjoint data.
Next up, episode fifteen: Case Studies, where we design a Parking Lot, a Vending Machine and a Coffee Machine end to end. See you there.
